## Dependency and security housekeeping

No feature changes in this release — nothing in the app looks or behaves any
differently. This is a maintenance pass on the third-party packages Training
Tracker is built from, prompted by the deprecation notices and the vulnerability
count that `update.sh` prints on every install.

Running an update now reports **no critical vulnerabilities** (previously one)
and **four high** (previously eight), with **two** deprecation notices instead of
three.

### Security fixes

- **Next.js updated to 16.3.4.** This is the important one. It closes two
  critical remote-code-execution advisories and around twenty further issues
  covering middleware/proxy bypasses, server-side request forgery, cache
  poisoning and denial of service. It also brings in patched versions of two
  bundled libraries (`postcss` and `sharp`) that carried their own advisories.
- **The email library updated to nodemailer 10.** Fixes five advisories,
  including one that allowed a crafted message to read local files or make
  requests to internal addresses, and two that let a carefully-formed recipient
  address bypass domain checks. This affects scheduled exports delivered by
  email.
- **The spreadsheet engine now comes from the vendor's own CDN.** The copy on
  the npm registry has been frozen for years on a release with two known
  security advisories (prototype pollution and a regular-expression denial of
  service) and no fix was ever published there. Training Tracker now installs it
  directly from the vendor instead, on a current, patched release. Excel imports
  and exports are unchanged — same behaviour, same file formats.

  **One thing to check if you run a locked-down network:** installs and updates
  now need outbound HTTPS to `cdn.sheetjs.com` in addition to
  `registry.npmjs.org`. If your firewall or proxy allow-lists hosts, add it
  before your next update. There is a note in the README's Troubleshooting
  section.

### Also

- **Google API client updated**, which removes one of the three deprecation
  notices at its source (an old, unmaintained file-handling library it used to
  pull in).
- **Five unused packages removed** from the install — two Microsoft
  authentication libraries, a date library, a database driver and a redundant
  set of type definitions. None of them were referenced anywhere in the app;
  they were left behind by earlier work and were being downloaded and installed
  on every deployment for nothing. Installs are correspondingly smaller.

### Known and deliberately left alone

Three items still show up and are worth explaining rather than hiding:

- **One of the two remaining deprecation notices** concerns a small helper
  package used deep inside the Google API client. It is a "this is built into
  modern Node.js now" notice, not a vulnerability, and it is present in every
  current version of that client — so there is nothing to upgrade to. Removing
  it would mean dropping the Google client entirely and hand-writing the Drive
  upload, which is not a change worth making for a cosmetic warning.
- **The code-linting tool stays on its current major version**, so its
  deprecation notice remains too. The newer version is available, but three of
  the plug-ins our Next.js lint preset depends on have not been updated for it
  yet — one of them crashes outright on every file. This was tried and reverted
  during this release rather than shipped broken. It is a development-time tool
  that is not part of the running application, and we will move it when the
  plug-ins catch up.
- **Four high-severity advisories remain**, all in the database toolkit's
  command-line tool. There is no fixed release on the version line we are on —
  the only available "fix" is a downgrade that this app cannot take. It is a
  build-time tool rather than part of the running application, and the specific
  vulnerable component is a MySQL driver that a PostgreSQL app never loads.
  We will pick up the fix when the next major version of that toolkit is
  released.
